In fact, option A—augmented with a union type rather than replacing the type with a function—is the better choice. The proposed version A would require you to provide a function every single time, even when you only need to specify a static value; while that might not seem like much extra typing, it would almost certainly become quite tiresome sooner or later.

Fair point, a union is more ergonomic and makes the change non-breaking for the vast majority of usages:

```ts
defaultValue?: NoInfer<T> | (() => NoInfer<T>)
```

The only catch is the ambiguity I mentioned in the proposal: when `T` is itself a function type, `defaultValue: someFn` would silently change meaning (it'd be called instead of returned as the value), with no compile error. That's the same trade-off React accepted with `useState(initial | () => initial)`.

That could be handled by combining both ideas: the union for the API, plus a much narrower migration that only rewrites the (rare) call sites where the resource's value type is a function, wrapping them as `defaultValue: () => fn` to preserve current behavior. Static defaults like `defaultValue: []` stay untouched.

> The only catch is the ambiguity I mentioned in the proposal: when T is itself a function type

That’s also a valid point; however, it can be easily resolved by explicitly specifying the generic type.

Fair question. I found it while reading the resource code, not in a production app. But it reproduces with the documented [`chain()` pattern](https://angular.dev/guide/signals/resource#chaining-resources), where `params` throws by design (`ResourceDependencyError`). User code doesn't throw anything:

```ts
const userResource = resource({
  params: () => ({id: 1}),
  loader: () => fetchUser(), // fails once, e.g. a 503
});

const companyResource = resource({
  params: ({chain}) => chain(userResource)?.companyId,
  loader: ({params}) => fetchCompany(params),
});
```

A "Retry" button on the company card calls `companyResource.reload()`:

| Step | `userResource` | `companyResource` | `companyResource.error()` | Company loader ran | `reload()` returned |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Initial | `error` | `error` | Dependency error | 0 | |
| Retry 1 | `error` | `idle` | Dependency error | 0 | `true` |
| Retry 2 | `error` | `idle` | Dependency error | 0 | `false` |
| `userResource.reload()` succeeds | `resolved` | `resolved` | none | 1 | |

So the UI switches from the error state to an empty `idle` state even though nothing loaded.

One correction to my description: it isn't permanently stuck. It recovers once `userResource` reloads successfully, because the params change. The bug is that `reload()` reports success without loading, and leaves `status()` and `error()` disagreeing.

I'd expect `reload()` to return `false` and keep the `error` state when the error comes from `params`. I'm happy to send a PR if that's the behaviour you'd want.

I think that if a resource sets itself into error-state after an initial crash in params, the resource should not have undefined behaviour in this case either.

While it's true that standard browsers reflect popover, inert, and max from IDL properties to content attributes, Angular's template binding model fundamentally targets DOM properties (el[name] = value), not HTML attributes.

Domino was designed as a lightweight DOM for SSR serialization, not a full WHATWG IDL compliance engine. Trying to manually maintain browser reflection parity in Domino for every newly standardized property is an endless maintenance burden.

Furthermore, several of these properties (like popoverTargetElement or commandForElement) take element references in IDL, which cannot be reflected to HTML attributes anyway.

For properties that are strictly 1:1 reflected attributes needed for initial SSR render (like popover or inert), updating Domino's reflection definitions may be a practical fix for now, but we should be cautious about adding complex spec-validation getters (e.g. clamping meter values or parsing command keywords) into Domino.
Related: a fix for the same mismatch exists as an unmerged commit, bb6d0109a073a3a9d9db2e69686d0c91d2d1b4ff (for #67241). See the discussion on #71617.

static classes are valid selectors for content projection, we should probably not regress on this.

> static classes are valid selectors for content projection, we should probably not regress on this.

Agreed, and that’s kept: NG8031 doesn’t report static attributes, class included, on a node that a specific `<ng-content select>` slot selects. Slot matching includes class names, so `select=".card-body"` counts. A static class is reported only when no directive matches the node and no specific slot selects it, which is when it has no effect. I’ll add a test for the class case to #71882.
Fyi, About `ng-template` I was testing things on #71887 and it raised a behavior that was implemented by #53457.

> Fyi, About `ng-template` I was testing things on [#71887](https://github.com/angular/angular/pull/71887) and it raised a behavior that was implemented by [#53457](https://github.com/angular/angular/pull/53457).

Thanks for flagging it. #71882 keeps that behavior. On an explicit `<ng-template>`, it treats `[attr.x]`, `[class.x]`, and `[style.x]` as property bindings named `x`, as the compiler has done since #53457 ([`compilesToProperty`](https://github.com/Flarette/angular/blob/0747cac2983d4a4a9bbb69526e5693680a279f3e/packages/compiler/src/typecheck/ops/ignored_bindings.ts#L147-L162)). A directive input named `x` claims them, so NG8031 only reports the ones nothing claims.

Covered in [`ignored_bindings_spec.ts`](https://github.com/Flarette/angular/blob/0747cac2983d4a4a9bbb69526e5693680a279f3e/packages/compiler-cli/test/ngtsc/ignored_bindings_spec.ts#L285-L299):
- `should not report a class binding on ng-template` (`p-input-dir [class.p]`)
- `should not report a style binding on ng-template` (`p-input-dir [style.p]`)
- `should not report an attribute binding on ng-template` (`p-input-dir [attr.p]`)
- `should report a class binding on ng-template` and `should report an attribute binding on ng-template` (no directive claims them)

The `ng_template_bindings` compliance test from #53457 stays as it is.

They need to be re-measured, optimized and deleted regularly or they just become the context bloat. In fact some people say to avoid angular skills and use MCP only.

Thanks for the perspective, @Flarette. That's a fair concern about skills, but I think it's a separate question from what this proposal changes.

This doesn't add or change any skills. The skills in `skills/dev-skills` already exist and are already published. The proposal only adds two small manifest files so people who want those skills can install them through the Claude Code and Codex plugin marketplaces, instead of copying files by hand.

- **No context cost unless installed:** nothing is loaded unless someone chooses to install it. Anyone who prefers MCP only, or thinks skills are bloat, is unaffected.
- **Easy to remove:** if skills turn out not to be worth keeping, deleting two manifest files is trivial. If the skills are removed or pruned, the manifests go with them.
- **You're right that skills need maintenance:** that's an argument for how the skills are curated, which this proposal doesn't touch. I'd be glad to help with that separately if useful.

So I'd frame it as: if the team keeps shipping these skills, is making them installable in one step reasonable? Happy to adjust the scope if the maintainers see it differently.

This issue (#71917) is about **cached response bodies** when `responseType === 'blob'` (for example, a `GET` request via `HttpClient.get(url, {responseType: 'blob'})` or `httpResource.blob()`). Since `GET` requests have `serializedBody === null`, PR #70227 still caches them, and `transferCacheInterceptorFn` still passes the `HttpResponse`'s `Blob` body to `toBase64()`, which runs `new Uint8Array(blob)` and stores `""` in `TransferState`.

Thanks for the context on #67002 / #67439, @SkyZeroZx — that's super helpful to know!

Looking at #67002, it passed an `async` callback directly to `concatMap(async (event) => ...)`, which turned **every** response (`json`, `text`, `arraybuffer`, etc.) into a `Promise` and broke synchronous `httpResource` / `hydration_spec` / `transfer_cache_spec` tests.

In my local fix, I avoided that by keeping the synchronous path via `of(event)` for all non-`Blob` responses and only returning `from(body.arrayBuffer())` when `responseType === 'blob' && body instanceof Blob`. With that change, all existing `httpResource`, `transfer_cache_spec`, `hydration_spec`, and `platform-server` tests continue to run synchronously and pass unmodified.

`@angular-devkit/build-angular:browser` does not natively support Module Federation or custom Webpack configurations. Using `ModuleFederationPlugin` requires modifying the internal Webpack configuration via a third-party builder (such as `@angular-architects/module-federation`), which is not supported by the Angular team. Additionally, the Webpack-based build pipeline (`browser` builder) is deprecated in favor of the `@angular/build:application` builder (which can be used with solutions like `@angular-architects/native-federation`).

Because this crash is caused by an upstream incompatibility between `webpack >= 5.107.0` and `license-webpack-plugin` when `ProvideSharedModule` is added to the Webpack compilation, we do not plan to fork or monkey-patch `license-webpack-plugin` in `@angular-devkit/build-angular`.

If a fix is released upstream in `license-webpack-plugin` (e.g., `4.0.3`), it will be picked up automatically by the existing `^4.0.2` version range. In the meantime, the recommended workarounds are:
- Migrating to the `@angular/build:application` builder and `@angular-architects/native-federation`
- Patching `license-webpack-plugin` locally (e.g., via `patch-package` or `pnpm patch`)
- Reporting this to `@angular-architects/module-federation`, as their builder could potentially adjust or wrap the plugin in the custom Webpack config.

A few points I would like to clarify here:

1. The premise that browser polyfills are fully explicit while server polyfills are implicit is not entirely accurate. The CLI already shapes the browser polyfills bundle depending on the project configuration. For instance, in JIT mode it injects `@angular/compiler`, when a source locale is defined it injects the locale data, and it removes `@angular/localize` when translation inlining is enabled. Similarly on the server side, polyfills are derived declaratively from the same application configuration. If an application is zoneless, Zone.js is omitted. If it is zoned, the appropriate node or neutral entry is used. If localize is configured, localize init is included. The `polyfills` option in `angular.json` is meant to define application level capabilities rather than low level bundle entry lists.

2. `ɵENABLE_DOM_EMULATION` is a private token used solely for internal framework benchmarks in the angular repository. In those benchmarks, the SSR code was executed inside a headless Chrome browser to measure rendering performance against a real DOM. Running outside a browser with DOM emulation disabled is explicitly rejected at runtime by platform server (`RuntimeError: 5704 (DISABLED_DOM_EMULATION_IN_NON_BROWSER)`). DOM emulation is required for Angular SSR to function, so providing an option to turn it off in server builds would expose an invalid and unsupported state.

3. `@angular/platform-server/init` is necessary for module evaluation time. While `DominoAdapter.makeCurrent()` applies DOM shims during platform initialization, `init` is needed before that when modules are first evaluated. Any top level code or third party dependency referencing DOM globals (such as `HTMLElement`, `customElements`, or `Event` in `@angular/elements` or web component libraries) will fail immediately with a `ReferenceError` when the server bundle loads if `init` is not present. Deferring this to platform initialization would also not keep `globalThis` clean, as Domino still mutates `globalThis` on the very first render request anyway.

4. The disk and heap overhead cited from #34514 is caused by Domino being bundled twice across independent build contexts. This is a separate bundling issue tracked in #34514. Because platform server requires Domino for `DominoAdapter` anyway, omitting `init` would not reduce the server bundle footprint because Domino would simply be bundled into the server chunk instead. The `init` module itself is only a few lines of code and adds negligible overhead.

5. Server polyfills are already supported through standard imports. Unlike browsers which depend on script tags injected into the HTML document, server applications already have explicit entry points. Runtime shims can be imported directly at the top of `src/server.ts`, and build time or SSG shims can be imported in `src/main.server.ts`.

Given the above, we do not plan to introduce user controllable server polyfills, and I will be closing this issue.

Hi @cracksalad,

To answer your questions:

1. **Pinning versions:** We deliberately pin dependencies in the CLI to guarantee deterministic builds and prevent unexpected regressions. With build tooling and compilers (such as Vite, esbuild, and TypeScript), upstream patch and minor updates frequently introduce subtle behavioral changes or breakages. Pinning ensures that what users install has been fully verified against our test suites. If an application needs an immediate patch before a CLI release, package manager overrides (npm or pnpm) or resolutions (yarn) can be used in the workspace `package.json`.

2. **Automated security scanning:** We already use automated tooling Renovate across the repository that tracks security advisories and opens PRs for dependency updates. While updates on LTS branches are handled more conservatively to maintain stability, we prioritize critical security updates whenever necessary.

3. **Release cadence**: We ship regular releases every Wednesday. If a critical zero-day vulnerability directly impacts the production runtime, we issue an immediate out-of-band release. However, for build-time tooling where high-severity CVEs often turn out to be false alarms or unexplainable in CLI usage we follow our regular weekly schedule to ensure thorough testing and validation before releasing

The same symptom has a second cause: the entry file of the chunk optimizer. The debug ID fix above does not fix it.

The chunk optimizer runs when an app has 3 or more lazy chunks. It renames the lazy chunks, and `main` imports them by name. But the optimizer passes `chunkFileNames` and no `entryFileNames`, so `main` keeps the name that esbuild gave it.

So when a builder release changes how the optimizer names chunks, the bytes of `main` change and its name stays the same. 22.2.6 did that with #34583.

```bash
npx @angular/cli@22.2.5 new repro --defaults --ssr=false
cd repro
npm install -D @angular/build@22.2.5
npx ng generate component a
npx ng generate component b
npx ng generate component c
cat > src/app/app.routes.ts <<'EOF'
import { Routes } from '@angular/router';

export const routes: Routes = [
  { path: 'a', loadComponent: () => import('./a/a').then((m) => m.A) },
  { path: 'b', loadComponent: () => import('./b/b').then((m) => m.B) },
  { path: 'c', loadComponent: () => import('./c/c').then((m) => m.C) },
];
EOF
npx ng config projects.repro.architect.build.configurations.production.sourceMap true
npx ng config projects.repro.architect.build.configurations.production.subresourceIntegrity true
npx ng build && mv dist/repro/browser ../build-22.2.5
npm install -D @angular/build@22.2.6
npx ng build && mv dist/repro/browser ../build-22.2.6
```

Both builds write `main-5H54S2WB.js`, and the two `index.html` files pin different hashes for it. The only difference in the file is the names of the chunks it imports:

```
build-22.2.5: chunk-jbVvGIzd.js chunk-BldQ8CJu.js chunk-BsxYmvae.js
build-22.2.6: chunk-Dn-U95iY.js chunk-Da40IlVd.js chunk-DZObh1Dd.js
```

The debug ID and the source map of `main` are the same in both builds.

A possible fix is to give the entry a content hash with `entryFileNames`, the same way as `chunkFileNames`, and to update `index.html` with the new name. A fix that computes every file name from its final bytes would cover both causes.

I looked at how to fix both causes. The fix for the second cause is small. The fix for the first cause has a trade-off that a maintainer should decide.

The rule I want to keep is that when the bytes of a hashed file change, its name changes too. That rule must also hold on the upgrade to the release that contains the fix.

### Second cause: the entry file of the chunk optimizer

The fix passes `entryFileNames` to the three `generate()` calls in `chunk-optimizer.ts`, so `main` gets a content hash when bundles are hashed. `initialFiles` then uses the new name. With `outputHashing: none`, the file stays `main.js`.

When the optimizer runs, the name of `main` can now contain lowercase letters, `_`, and `-`, as the names of the lazy chunks already do.

### First cause: the debug ID

The builder adds the debug ID line after esbuild picks the file name. If the builder computes the ID in a new way, the bytes of each file change and its name stays the same. The release that fixes this bug would therefore cause the same SRI failure one more time. It would affect apps that use script source maps and SRI and still have the old files in a cache.

I see these options:

1. Compute the debug ID from the file name and the JS. A later rewrite of the source map can no longer change the JS. The upgrade still breaks the rule once, so the release would need a note that tells users to purge cached JS.
2. Do option 1 and force a one-time rename. This needs a version comment in the esbuild bundles and a constant in `augmentChunkHash`. The upgrade is safe, but the bundles carry a comment that exists only to change a hash. I don't like this option.
3. Keep the current debug ID and name the files from their final bytes. This is the option I prefer.

Option 3 adds a step after `injectDebugIds`, only when bundles are hashed and script source maps are on. The step hashes each JS file with the names of the other output files replaced by a placeholder. It includes the hashes of the files that the JS file can reach through imports, as Rollup does to handle import cycles. It then renames the files and updates those names in the JS and the source maps. `initialFiles` and the metafile get the new names, so the index HTML, SRI, the SSR manifest, and the service worker use them.

With option 3, every file with a debug ID gets a new name once, on the upgrade. After that, any change to the bytes of those files changes the name, whatever the cause. The cost is more code, because the builder would rewrite file names inside generated code. Each locale also needs its own copy of `initialFiles` and the metafile, and the build stats table must print the final names.

Keeping the current debug ID without option 3 avoids the upgrade problem, but the bug comes back the next time the builder writes the source map differently.

Would you accept a rename step like option 3 in the application builder? I have not built it yet. If you would not, which other option do you prefer? I can open a PR for the second cause now and a PR for the first cause once you pick a direction.

Hi @ryuran, thanks for raising this suggestion!

Using `<svg><use href="#..."></use></svg>` with `<symbol>` is a classic technique for reducing DOM node count, but in the context of Angular Material, there are several known browser and architectural constraints that led to the current inlined cloning implementation:

1. **Client-side routing and `<base href>` breakages**:
   The maintainers actually noted this directly in [`icon-registry.ts`](https://github.com/angular/components/blob/main/src/material/icon/icon-registry.ts#L551-L554):
   > *"Note that the same could be achieved by referring to it via `<use href="#id">`, however the `<use>` tag is problematic on Firefox, because it needs to include the current page path."*
   
   In SPAs using HTML5 pushState routing or `<base href>`, relative fragment references (`#id`) break across page transitions unless dynamically rewritten with the full current pathname on every route change.

2. **CSS styling encapsulation**:
   Elements rendered through `<use>` exist in a closed user-agent shadow root. External CSS and component-scoped styles (such as `mat-icon path { fill: currentColor; }` or targeting specific child layers of multi-color icons) cannot penetrate the `<use>` boundary. Inlining the SVG nodes ensures that CSS styling, theme colors, and animations work as expected.

3. **Lifecycle & SSR/Hydration**:
   Managing a global `<svg>` definition sprite in the document body or head introduces state-management complexity, potential memory leaks when icons are registered dynamically, and hydration mismatches during server-side rendering.

Given these trade-offs, inlining the SVG node has remained the most reliable, cross-browser, and styleable solution. It would be interesting to hear the maintainers' current thoughts on whether an opt-in symbol strategy could ever be considered, or if these constraints still make it a non-starter.
